title: Migration 44 — the marketplace reservation ledger
description: Applies migrations 39 then 44, runs 44's VERIFY A-I, then rolls back 44 on a disposable PostgreSQL 18 cluster. First migration of the Option B marketplace, written to docs/OPTION_B_SEAM_CONTRACT.md so that adding physical custody later is a plug-in and not a rewrite. The obvious design -- an inventory_batches.reserved_kg column decremented on reservation -- fails three ways at once: it loses its own history when written, two concurrent buyers both read it before either writes, and when Option A introduces lots that SPLIT the identity the number hangs off stops existing. So a reservation is a row, a release is another row, and availability is a SUM evaluated when asked, exactly as migration 40 already does for permit draw-down. Expiry is computed for the same reason licence expiry is: this repository has no scheduler at all, so a stored expiry flag would be exactly as fresh as a job that never runs. Reservations are commercial events, so 44 creates its own commercial_audit_log instead of forcing open compliance_audit_log's closed regulatory vocabulary.

verify.note: J is the regression guard for the audit separation: reservations are COMMERCIAL events, so migration 44 creates commercial_audit_log rather than widening compliance_audit_log's closed 15-value regulatory vocabulary (target architecture 2.6 / gap item MC-18). A closed vocabulary is only worth having if it was never opened, so J asserts the compliance constraint admits neither reservation action, that no reservation row reaches the compliance log, and that the commercial log is append-only with its own closed vocabulary and writable by no client role. C is the section that proves the design rather than the code: it places a hold that lapses in an hour, then asks for availability as at two hours later and requires the full quantity back -- with the reservation row unmutated and no release record written, because expiry that is DERIVED cannot go stale and expiry that is STORED always can. G is the NaN guard in its marketplace form: PostgreSQL sorts numeric NaN above every real number, so an unguarded comparison would treat a NaN-quantity batch as having effectively infinite stock; it also asserts the ledger never writes inventory_batches.stock_status, which would be a second source of truth going stale the instant a hold expired. F proves the refusals AND the equivalent valid reservation, so the refusals cannot be artefacts of a broken fixture. H is behavioural under SET ROLE authenticated and covers the double-blind rule in both directions -- a buyer sees their own reservations but cannot reach the batch row, the farm organisation or supply-side demand; a farmer sees NO reservation rows at all yet still gets the reserved quantity for their own batch through a function. NOT read-only; wrapped in BEGIN..ROLLBACK. NOT PROVEN HERE: that the FOR UPDATE lock serialises genuinely concurrent reservations -- a single session cannot demonstrate that and it needs a two-session test on staging before the marketplace opens.
